# User studies

Use this file when asked to plan a study or interpret supplied, authorized participant or metric
material. It grants no recruitment, recording, upload, external read, or product-action permission;
the skill's source-access limits remain unchanged. A protocol is planned work, not executed research.
Never simulate participants and label the result findings, invent quotations or saturation, or send
sensitive raw notes to an unauthorized service. Keep decisions in the project's existing record.

## Choose evidence for the decision

Name the decision, population/circumstance, unresolved question, and observation that would change
it before choosing a method. Different methods expose different limits:

| Question | Useful method | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| Actual workflow and constraints | Contextual inquiry | Access and observation can alter behavior |
| Goals, vocabulary, or mental model | Recent-episode interview | Recall and social desirability |
| Task breakdown | Moderated task study | Script and prototype constrain behavior |
| Attitude prevalence | Survey with a sampling plan | Self-report and nonresponse |
| Grouping versus finding | Card sort, then tree/task test | A grouping preference is not navigation success |
| Intermittent or changing behavior | Diary study | Burden and attrition |
| Recorded drop-off or recurrence | Audited analytics | Instrumentation shows events, not motive |
| Causal variant comparison | Planned randomized experiment | Power, contamination, and guardrail assumptions |

Do not triangulate with methods sharing the same blind spot. Recruit by relevant behavior, role,
expertise, language, disability, and operating context; disclose missing groups. Participant counts
follow population diversity, stakes, method, effect/precision, and stopping rule—not a universal
five-person threshold. A small formative round can find a revision without estimating prevalence.
Consent covers activities, observers, processing, optional recording/reuse, withdrawal, and policy;
it is not blanket permission for later recipients. Collect minimally and use approved storage.

## Preserve the protocol's meaning

Separate formative discovery, stable-release benchmarking, comparative studies, longitudinal work,
and experiments before collecting data. Give a plausible goal and starting state without teaching
interface labels or the path. Use safe synthetic task data; pilot the script and define assistance,
intervention, exclusion, and end conditions. Think-aloud supports diagnosis but can distort timing.
Record assisted, partial, and independent completion separately; an alternate safe path is not an
error merely because it differs from the expected one. A static prototype proves no runtime input,
network, or assistive-technology behavior.

Operationalize each measure: eligible unit, numerator, denominator, time window, task version,
missing/excluded data, and uncertainty. Audit duplicate/retry/offline/test events; separate exposure,
use, and success. Follow goal → signal → metric with counter-signals and harm/access/support
constraints. More engagement or fewer clicks need not mean greater user value.

For a standardized perceived-usability questionnaire, retain its validated wording, scoring, timing,
and translation and cite that version. Its normalized score is neither a percent of usability met,
a diagnosis, nor an accessibility pass; comparison bands require their actual dataset. A benchmark
requires a comparable population and protocol. Experiments predeclare outcome, randomization unit,
meaningful effect, power, guardrails, duration, and stopping/analysis rules; never stop at a pleasing
result or withhold a required safety/access fix to create a control.

## Synthesize without upgrading evidence

Keep observation, interpretation, opportunity, and recommendation distinct and traceable to the
anonymized source and context. Preserve contradictions, negative cases, and segment differences.
A quote illustrates a theme, affinity clusters do not establish prevalence, and a convenience poll
is not representative. Behavioral archetypes include only evidence-linked attributes that change
a decision; unobserved journey stages and emotions remain unknown. Report protocol, version,
participants, devices, dates, assistance, limits, and the next evidence-dependent decision.
